client: I've been feeling really guilty lately because my partner keeps saying we're growing apart. I know they're right—I've been working late almost every night—but I'm terrified of falling behind at my job. Part of me wonders if talking about this will even help when the real problem is just that there aren't enough hours in the day.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy weight of guilt and fear—caught between wanting to nurture your relationship and meeting work demands. When you say "there aren't enough hours in the day," what thoughts come up about what might need to change to create more balance?

client:
I just feel like no matter what I do, I'm failing someone. If I stay late at work, I'm letting my partner down. If I leave on time, I'm not meeting deadlines. The thought of trying to "balance" it all just makes me more anxious because it feels impossible. 

I guess part of me knows something has to change, but every option seems bad—either I disappoint my boss or I hurt my relationship. It's like I'm trapped.
therapist: You're describing that painful feeling of being stuck between two impossible choices, where every path seems to lead to disappointment. That sense of being trapped often comes from seeing things in all-or-nothing terms—have you noticed any moments where there might have been small compromises or middle grounds that got overlooked?

client:
I don't know... when I try to think of middle grounds, it just feels like I'd be settling for something that still makes me unhappy. Like if I choose either option, I'm betraying part of myself. It's not that simple to just find compromises when both choices feel so emotionally loaded. 

I keep going in circles thinking about this - part of me knows there should be a better way, but another part feels like any solution will just leave me feeling guilty or resentful. Maybe I'm just not seeing what you're seeing.
therapist:
It sounds like you're caught in a really difficult tug-of-war between these two important parts of your life, where every potential solution still feels like a loss. That frustration of going in circles is completely understandable when both choices carry such deep emotional weight. 

What do you think might happen if we stepped back from trying to solve the whole problem at once, and instead looked for one small area where you could experiment with a tiny adjustment?

client:
I get what you're saying about small adjustments, but honestly even that feels overwhelming right now. Every time I try to make any change, my brain immediately jumps to all the ways it could go wrong or how it might hurt one side of this situation. 

I guess I could try something tiny, but I'm worried that starting small will just feel pointless when the bigger problem is still hanging over me.
therapist:
I hear how overwhelming even small changes feel when the bigger picture still feels so heavy—it's like trying to patch a leak when the whole dam feels ready to burst. That fear of things going wrong makes complete sense when both your relationship and career feel so important. 

What would feel like a manageable first step—something so small that even if it didn't work perfectly, it wouldn't feel catastrophic?

client:
I don't know... even small steps feel risky right now. If I try reaching out to my partner more and they're still distant, it'll just confirm my fear that things are falling apart. And at work, if I speak up in a meeting and stumble over my words, everyone will think I'm incompetent. The stakes feel too high to mess up at all. 

Maybe just... making a list of what I want to say first? But even that seems pointless when I know I'll probably chicken out when the moment comes.
therapist:
I can see how even preparing to take action feels scary when you're anticipating things going wrong—it's like your mind is already bracing for disappointment before anything happens. That fear of confirming your worst worries makes it so hard to take even the smallest steps forward.  

Making a list actually sounds like a thoughtful first move—not as something that has to lead to immediate action, but as a way to start sorting through these heavy thoughts. What would it feel like to write things down without any pressure to act on them right away?

client:
I guess writing things down without pressure does sound less overwhelming, but part of me worries that just seeing my anxious thoughts on paper will make them feel more real. What if the list just confirms how many things I'm scared of? 

I also keep thinking that if I don't act on the problems right away, I'm being lazy or avoiding them. That guilt makes it hard to just observe my thoughts without judging myself.
therapist:
It makes sense that putting thoughts on paper might feel like giving them more power, especially when you're already carrying so much self-judgment about needing to "fix" things immediately. That pressure to act right away sounds exhausting—like you can't even pause to understand the problem without feeling guilty.  

What if we framed the list differently—not as proof of your fears, but as a way to start separating which worries feel most urgent from ones that might be less pressing? Could that feel any more manageable?

client: I get what you're saying about separating urgent worries from less pressing ones, but honestly, even making that list feels overwhelming. What if I get it wrong and end up focusing on the wrong things? I already second-guess myself constantly, and now I'm supposed to rank my anxieties like some kind of priority to-do list? It just makes me feel like I'm setting myself up to fail at yet another thing.
therapist:
I hear how even the idea of organizing your worries brings up that familiar fear of getting it wrong—it's like your mind keeps adding extra layers of "what ifs" to every possible step forward. That self-doubt makes everything feel so much heavier than it needs to be.  

What if we took the pressure off completely? Instead of ranking or judging the worries, what would it feel like to just notice them—like clouds passing by—without needing to do anything about them yet?

client:
I get what you're saying about just noticing the worries, but it's hard to imagine them just passing by like clouds. When I try that, they don't feel light or temporary—they feel heavy and urgent, like they're screaming for my attention. 

And honestly, the idea of not doing anything about them makes me more anxious, like I'm ignoring something important that could blow up later.
therapist:
It makes complete sense that these worries feel so loud and demanding—when they carry such real weight in your life, they're not going to just float away easily. That fear of them "blowing up" shows how much these concerns matter to you, even as they exhaust you.  

What if we tried something different: instead of trying to dismiss them or act on them immediately, what would it feel like to acknowledge just one worry by saying, "I hear you, and we'll address this when the time is right"?

client: That sounds nice in theory, but when I try to acknowledge my worries like that, they just come back stronger. It's like telling a kid "later" - they just keep pestering you more. I feel like if I don't deal with the thoughts right away, they'll spiral out of control.
therapist:
I hear how those worries keep demanding your attention—it's like they don't trust that "later" will ever come, so they push harder to be heard now. That fear of spiraling makes it so hard to pause, even when you're exhausted.  

What do you think would happen if we explored what makes these particular thoughts feel so urgent? Like, what's the worst-case scenario they're trying to protect you from?

client:
I guess the worst case is that if I don't keep worrying about everything, I'll miss some important danger or problem. Like if I relax for even a second, something terrible will happen that I could have prevented. But honestly, just saying that out loud makes me realize how exhausting it is to live like this. 

I don't know how to trust that things will be okay without constantly monitoring everything. It feels irresponsible to stop worrying, even though I know it's making me miserable.
therapist:
It sounds like you're realizing how much energy this constant vigilance takes—that painful contradiction between knowing the worry is draining you, yet fearing that letting go would be reckless. That's such a difficult space to be in.  

What comes up for you when you imagine that middle ground—where you could care about these important parts of your life *without* feeling solely responsible for preventing every possible bad outcome?
